utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Now, the Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey. Defence teams, I don't know -- there is Mr. Ostojic missing. And is Ms. Nikolic here or not? Yes, Ms. Nikolic is here, but I couldn't see you behind the column. And that's about it. I think everyone else is present, Mr. Sarapa as well. Okay. According to where we left things yesterday, apart from the task that you undertook yourself, Mr. Haynes, in relation to your client, which I hope was a successful one, the plan was for you to start with your opening statement this morning, lasting approximately 20 minutes or thereabouts, and then proceed with the testimony of your client. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So you have the floor, Mr. Haynes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned colleagues and friends, ladies and gentlemen, I don't know precisely when I first undertook the task of presenting a case in a court of law, but suffice it to say for 20-odd years I've plied this trade, and yet today I find myself entering uncharted waters, because I have never previously opened a case for the Defence. The reasons for that, as you may know, are principally because of the rules which govern the system to which I'm most accustomed, and but also because of the culture in which I was educated. I frankly confess, therefore, that I don't really know what the task is that lies ahead of me. I used to think I knew what a Prosecution opening speech should sound like. That was at least until I arrived here and appreciated that in this jurisdiction, the Prosecution gets to make two opening speeches. It seems like an age ago now that we were first entertained to an address by Mrs. Carla Del Ponte, followed by something rather more regular and familiar to my ear from Mr. McCloskey. I recall at the time being mildly irritated by the idea of two addresses by the Prosecution, but I was raw and younger then, and I didn't then anticipate that I would say, about Mrs. Del Ponte's speech what I will say about it this morning, which is it was a fine piece of advocacy, and it was entirely appropriate that an historic trial of this nature should be put in an historic context. In truth, it was a privilege to have been there to hear it. And if you'll forgive me for just a few minutes, I would like, in common with the remarks made by a number of those who have gone before me, to develop that particular theme. It is truly a privilege and an honour to have this opportunity to appear before this Tribunal, and it is a privilege and an honour at every level. It is perhaps most apposite that of all the counsel in the case, I should acknowledge that, since whatever the outcome in my client's case, this experience has already rewarded me professionally and personally in a very concrete way. My gratitude to the Trial Chamber and my learned colleagues, who had a direct hand in the events of exactly a year ago today, are indelible and beyond my powers of expression. It's been a great learning curve. I do not recognise myself as the same criminal court hack who first arrived here nearly three years ago. I have had to learn about events of history, international justice, new concepts of criminal liability, and the complexities of the hardware and software of this, the most sophisticated court on the planet. In the presentation of my case, I am grateful not only to my co-counsel, but also to a team of energetic, intelligent, and resourceful young people. I have been proud to know and know will achieve whatever they want in life. No lawyer could decline the invitation to test his skills in an international tribunal, and it's been an honour thus far to work with the array of global talent that sits around me in this room. There is no doubt that you have to be on your game in this Trial Chamber, and some of the work that I have seen done by those in this court has been good enough to merit an entry fee. And whilst there has been the odd candidate for those lists of the most stupid questions ever asked by a lawyer, that was probably inevitable in a trial of this length, and I'll put it down to fatigue. Mr. President, it is no mean feat to manage a case of this substance and size, and you very nearly achieved it. You, the Judges, have set the tone for these proceedings, and you did so at the outset. The bywords have been tolerance, common sense, and humanity, and you're to be applauded for that. To the various other agencies of the Tribunal, whose cooperation and support has been constant and willing, I wish to convey my thanks publicly, and I acknowledge, too, the great dignity with which the victims and witnesses in this trial have recounted their difficult ordeals, and the dignity with which the accused have faced their trial. I had a series of goals at the outset of this case: to finish it in good health, solvent, still married, and in silk. We haven't got to the end yet, but I can check two out of four. I'll keep you posted as to the rest. The other ambition I had was to secure the best conceivable result for my client, Vinko Pandurevic, and I suppose I better start turning to that now, because no small part of the honour and the privilege I have described thus far has been the honour and the privilege to know and to represent him. Now, given that as I understand it, the function of an opening address is to set out the case that is about to be advanced in evidence, I will start with the rather prosaic job of giving you the program of events which we intend for the next few weeks. This may involve Your Honours considering various housekeeping matters during the course of the next day or so. As you know and have known, I submit, for some considerable time, the case of the seventh accused on this indictment will commence with the evidence of the accused, himself, in his own defence. Given the estimates of time for his examination, it appears inevitable that his evidence will consume not only the rest of this month, but the whole of February and perhaps a good portion of March as well. By that time, we will have been sitting for perhaps eight or nine weeks in this year, although I observe from the court calendar a few spare days next week, but I suspect, nonetheless, we would all probably welcome a break. We are going to invite the Trial Chamber to break for a week at the end of General Pandurevic's evidence. That will not represent a holiday for us, his Defence team, as we will be working on the presentation of further evidence. Of course, once we have heard his evidence, we will know more clearly where the issues are truly joined between the parties, and we will be able to decide which witnesses additional to the accused we still need and wish to call to give evidence. It is highly likely that we will, at that stage, substantially prune our witness list. Of course, we will keep our options open as long as possible, but have no fear we have no intention of doing a Gvero. We will make sure that everybody is informed in a timely fashion of what they can expect so that resources are not needlessly expended. We hope, moreover, that this matter can be agreed upon at an early stage so that judicial resources and the courtroom itself can be put to profitable use, if needed. Now, a number of practical matters arise from the fact that General Pandurevic will give evidence in his own defence, and I want to go back only briefly to the debate we had which occupied the whole of yesterday's proceedings. As an accused giving evidence in his own defence, General Pandurevic will have contact with his counsel to a greater or lesser degree throughout the course of that process. When, in the spring of last year, we placed his name upon his Rule 65 ter witness list, we could not anticipate that. When we did, and we genuinely did from the word "go," intend to call him to give evidence, we thought, that that period would, for him and I, be a period of splendid isolation, and I can tell you for one that I did regard an absence of visits from the Detention Unit in Scheveningen as splendid. But then in September, the Appeals Chamber in Prlic changed the law. Plain and simple, that's what they did. As counsel before this Tribunal, it is my minimal professional duty to keep abreast of changes in the law in this jurisdiction and my minimal professional duty to advise my client of changes in the law in this jurisdiction. You might think that General Pandurevic would be little short of insane if he didn't avail himself of what, after the 5th of September last year, became his legal right. Accused have many legal rights. Perhaps the most famous of them all is the one which the other six accused are exercising; namely, the right to sit in the dock and have the case proved against them. That could not be, in my submission, the subject of any inference or adverse comment. More still, we say, it would be utterly inappropriate were the process of General Pandurevic having access to his lawyer, which is his legal right, to attract inference or adverse comment in this case, because all he's doing is exercising a proper legal right. And I thought it appropriate to say that now because we are in new territory and because I sensed a certain flavour in yesterday's debate. I would also say this: I do hope that people will remember that if any discourse does take place, the other participant is likely to be me, and we've all enjoyed good relations during the course of this case, and I would be dismayed were unfounded or wild allegations were to arise during the course of anybody's examination of the General. I'll move on. As an accused, of course, it's General Pandurevic's right to be present at all times during his trial. That's why you, as the Judges in this case, are so careful to ensure that his consent to absence is properly recorded on occasions when he is, for example, sick. I only mention this because whilst I will genuinely try not to offend anybody in the questions I ask him, if there is any objection taken to the propriety of any line of examination, any debate about that and any decision must be conducted in his presence and to his full understanding. There will be no question of his either leaving the room or taking off his headphones. One last practical matter, and that is the question of the duration of the two longer sessions in any court day. These have routinely been of 90 minutes, but it has been my observation that statistically the most mistakes, the most misunderstandings, and the silliest squabbles between counsel have all occurred in the last ten minutes of those longer sessions. This is to nobody's advantage, and in my submission, has actually resulted in a loss of time. I invite you to the view that during General Pandurevic's evidence, the longest session should be of 80 minutes. The breaks would be of the same length. We don't lose any court time, and it will reduce the risk of fatigue on either his or our parts. Lastly on that note, I will, of course, keep a careful eye on the health and energy of my client and keep you fully appraised of any difficulties which may arise. He is, of course, a robust man, but he is past 50, and he is not without certain ancient health problems largely arising from the multiple injuries he received during the war. The remarks I will now make will not include a summary of the evidence that I'm going to call. That would be an insult to your intelligence. What I say does not have the force of evidence. What my client says will do. More to the point, you don't need me to tell you what my case is. I hope you know very well what my case is. You see, I am an Englishman. I was brought up to believe that the game of cricket was a design for life, that the music of the Beetles showed the true possibilities of the human condition and that the taste of single malt revealed the existence of God himself. I won't go as far as to say that baseball, bourbon, and Bruce Springsteen leave me cold. They're just not part of my makeup, that's all. As an English lawyer, I was raised at the alter of putting your case, and I believe we have done that explicitly throughout this trial wherever we could. I confess there are examples where we did not because no witness was called who could contradict the case we will now present. There were also occasions when you made me cut short my cross-examination and thus did not permit me to put certain things, but to the vast majority, we have been completely up-front throughout this case as to the evidence we would present for our client. The requirement to put your case is, in fact, incorporated in the Rules of the Tribunal. However, it appears it is given, rather like certain provisions of the brigade rules, a creative interpretation in certain quarters. It will be interesting to see how explicit the parties put their cases to General Pandurevic. Will the Prosecution, for example, make plain which aspects of PW-168's evidence it positively asserts to be true and which it abandons, or will they simply duck the issue? No less interesting will be the position of others, whose lines may be cut by the evidence of my client. Will they tell us what their case is, or will they simply seek to throw mud from behind a smoke-screen? Whether they should be permitted to do so is something that I will come to later. Now, you would be forgiven for asking, If he's not going to tell us what his case is, why is he wasting our time now?" Well, I suppose firstly because it would be a shame to go through a whole professional career without making an opening speech for a defendant, but secondly because there are a few things which I want to address in advance of your hearing the evidence. Nobody would deny that there has been, these last couple of days, a certain frisson in the atmosphere of the Trial Chamber. This is a moment of true excitement, the first and only accused in this trial to give evidence, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade whose forces took part in the taking of Srebrenica, and whose responsibility it was to defend the villages closest to many of the execution sites in the indictment, the brigade who fought with the 28th Division, the man who let thousands of men walk to freedom, in contravention of his orders from his superiors, the author of the Zvornik Brigade combat reports of the 15th, 16th, and 18th of July. It is a compelling and important story he has to tell. And he has the courage to tell it, and that's a lot of courage. It may only be 15 metres to walk from where he sits now to where he'll be sitting in a few minutes, but it's a short walk nobody else here had the guts even to contemplate. Of course, I dare say they see it rather differently, but Vinko Pandurevic has never been afraid to stand up to that sort of attitude, never been afraid to question authority, never been afraid to do what he thought was the right thing to do. He will take that walk in the full knowledge that nothing will ever be the same again. He does so publicly, not in closed or private session. He does so without guarantees as to his maximum liability in terms of his sentence. He does so as the first witness in his case, not holding back to see how it goes and where the gaps might appear, but by strapping on his protective clothing and going out to open the innings before he can possibly know how the pitch will play. He does so in the certain anticipation of all the attendant discomfort he will bring upon himself here and his family abroad. You will, of course, notice that the man who will take that walk has a few more kilos and rather a lot less hair than the 1995 model. He is also older, wiser, and of greater military rank than the 33-year-old captain who took command of the Zvornik Brigade in December 1992. I have known him for three years, and he is, if I may be forgiven for saying so, every inch a general. He walks the walk, and he talks the talk. Please do remember that a goodly portion of his knowledge, his experience, and his aura are after-acquired. When you look at the rather gauche individual who, on the trial video, attempted to stand up to General Mladic in the streets of Srebrenica, and was pre-emptorily dismissed, it is hard to imagine that it is the same Vinko Pandurevic that will be talking to us in a few minutes' time. I ask you please to retain that image, together with an impression of the rather childish and evasive behaviour he indulged in on July the 16th when the superior command wanted to know what he was up to, to counter-balance the impression of gravitus he may now display. Aspects of Vinko Pandurevic's character have surfaced in this case really from the very beginning, when he was described in complementary terms by Mr. McCloskey in his opening statement. Since then, witnesses have periodically and often quite unexpectedly broke out in praise of his personal qualities or his abilities as a soldier. I am not going to present him today to you as a great man or even as a good man. That is not because I don't think he is. I just don't think it matters in a case like this, one way or the other. These are the most serious criminal charges imaginable, and you are not going to acquit him on the basis that he is or might be a good son to his mother, any more than you are going to convict him because he was or might have been a bad husband to his first wife. We have been treated to a lot of cross-examination in this case, justified on the basis that it goes to a witness's character or credibility, and in my submission a good portion of it has been ill-directed and even gratuitous. It has gone largely unchecked in the past, but during the course of our case, we will be asking you to watch it rather more closely. You see, to give a slightly ridiculous example: If a witness comes to court merely to say General Mladic was drinking a beer in the streets of Srebrenica, it is not open to the lawyer of any party to assassinate his character, where the fact that General Mladic was drinking a beer in Srebrenica is not the subject of any challenge. That is not only irrelevant cross-examination, it is improper in the true sense of the word, and certainly, in my book, unethical. We are not afraid. My client and any witness called on his behalf will face down any proper test of credibility. But we are also not naive, and I don't necessarily address these remarks to the Bench's opposite. When we hear, for example, of investigators looking into the financial affairs of our client's wider family, and delving around in his ancient personal life, it is not too difficult to work out what they are up to and, ans indeed, who is up to it, and we're accordingly put on our guard. Such attacks, if they are sought to be made, we will say will have to be justified. We will ask, "What is the relevance of this?" And if the justification is credibility, we will say, "Credibility as to what? What is it you challenge? What do you say this man or this woman is lying about, and are you going to present a positive case on that issue?" The general and principal benefit to us all of General Pandurevic giving evidence is that there will be evidence in his case. On critical issues, you will not be struggling to draw inferences in a vacuum by documents of differing grades of probity. You will have his word and his explanation. Much of what he will say will simply confirm other evidence in the case, but some of what he will tell you will be entirely new to everybody. There are things that only he can tell you and things that are not recorded anywhere except in his memory. For useful they were told the officer's log-book was, not everything was recorded in it. Not every conversation on a radio was intercepted, and you have not heard evidence from all the people he met and spoke to in those critical days. Almost uniquely in this case, he will be able to speak to documents of which he was the author, and about recorded conversations in which he participated. Where he speaks to documents he wrote, he will tell you what he meant. We submit that it is imperative that you bear in mind where the burden of proof lies and remains throughout this case. He doesn't have to persuade you that when he says he meant one thing or another in a document, that that is correct. The effect of his evidence, however, in our submission, is to present the Prosecution with a mountain to climb to prove that he, the author, meant something else. And we submit that Mr. Richard Butler's opinions as to the meaning of a translated document he cannot even cite accurately in his report doesn't even get close. In considering the meaning of documents with General Pandurevic, you may find you are driven from time to time to question the adequacy of the English translation. It is not easy. Not every word in every language can find a direct translation into another. There are often numerous possibilities, each of which would subtly or even significantly affect the sense of a document. The Eskimos have 23 words for "snow." A translator can only translate those 23 words into one thing in English, and which one of the 23 do you pick when you are attempting the reverse exercise? The odds are heavily in favour of your losing the sense of the piece. And so we will see, when we come to certain documents in this case, and important documents, many concepts have different modes of expression. We will invite you to the view that it would be quite wrong to cling to a dampness valiant, though perhaps clumsy translation of a document, in the face of an explanation from its author as to its true meaning. I must just say one thing about translation, while we're on the subject, and it's something that has troubled me really since the outset of this case and has continued to trouble me. There is a phrase which appears in a large number of the documents in the case. It routinely appears in italicised letters inside oblique brackets, and the phrase is a derogatory term for Bosnian Muslims. Now, this phrase was not inserted by a single translator. Indeed, given the period of time spanning the various documents which have been treated to this commentary, it must have been inserted by successive generations of translators, and they did not all, over those years, sit independently at their desks and decide that you, the Judges of this Tribunal, and us, the practitioners, were so naive and inexperienced that we needed an explanation of the translation of one of two or three words. One is driven to the inescapable conclusion that this phrase has been inserted as a matter of policy. That must be right. Why you would, as a body of translators, have such a policy, we can probably only guess at. The absence of the phrase -- derogatory term for Serbs is stark where similar racial ethnic epithets are used. It's truly unfortunate. The effect of it is to flavour the Tribunal's records. I fear that in years to come, the practice may come to be seen by some as a symbol of something sinister, and what is wrong about it is that whether a word in any given context is derogatory, complementary, or somewhere in between, is a judgement, and you're the Judges, not the Translation Service, and somebody, Mr. President, sitting where you sit now should along time ago have said, "Stop it." Now, what's the point of all this? We live in a politically-correct world. We can all agree that reference to anybody by racial epithet is not good for society. It doesn't help us all get along together. But nothing was further from the minds of the inhabitants of Bosnia in the 1990s, and probably still now, than political correctness. Survival was probably the first of their worries. And as to the use of these terms, if your father has been murdered, your sister has been raped, and your house has been burned down, you're not going to refer to the people who did it as "friend," are you? You're probably not even going to call them "enemy." And I understand that part of the criticism made by the Prosecution is that at higher political and military levels, you have a greater degree of responsibility, but even in the most modern context, in times of war the demonisation of the enemy is a standard military tactic. We see that in the rhetoric of modern-day America on a daily basis. I invite you to the view that the use of epithets based on racial or ethnic origins during the course of this war tells you nothing about anybody. It certainly is no basis to disbelieve their evidence, and is certainly no basis for founding the requisite intent for the crimes charged on the indictment. Now, a veritable library has been written about the structure and management of the Yugoslav National Army and, to a lesser extent, the Army of Republika Srpska. They have been trawled before you in -- over months and months and months, and I confess as part of my case, you will see them again. But we would commend to you your own Statute, jurisprudence, and your perception of the evidence in coming to your decisions on culpability. Look rather to establish who it can be found in fact took part in events and what unit or units that or those people belonged to. Try and deduce whose orders they must have been following. That, we say, will serve you better than an in-depth study of books of rules, because to a great extent, stating the obvious, no rules could have anticipated the events which are the subject of this indictment, and you may conclude that the rules truly went out of the window. In shaping this address and shaping General Pandurevic's evidence, it would have been surprising if we hadn't taken a glance, at least, at the indictment. It has been described by others in the past as complex. Insofar as it describes myriad forms of criminal liability, each overlaying upon the other, I suppose that is a description which could be supplied to it. Our review of it has led us to a rather different conclusion. In our submission, when you come to the particulars of the indictment and the allegations it makes, it's a cowardly document. It's a cowardly document because it shies away from making the allegation that it should make. It doesn't tell you who was truly in command of events on the ground. It doesn't tell you who was telling the soldiers to shoot the prisoners at the various execution sites, and that is critical to an understanding of General Pandurevic's case, because he was not, we submit, in command of the people who were killing prisoners at Rocevic or Petkovski. They came from units all over the place. There was somebody there, a senior officer, but the indictment neglects to allege that or those men were in command. It shies away from it. Now, there may be tactical or historical reasons for that. It may be to cause the allegations in this case to fit more comfortably with the positions of others. I don't know why Dragan Obrenovic pleaded guilty. Men take courses such as that for all sorts of reasons. It might have seemed to him an expedient measure. It might have seemed to him the best thing to do. He might have wanted certainty. But that should in no way be some sort of impediment to your fair and proper consideration of his commander, Vinko Pandurevic. He will now take you on a journey inside the workings of the Zvornik Brigade, a brigade like no other in an army like no other. He will tell you what it was truly like to be the commander of that brigade, what his soldiers were like, and the madness that greeted him on the 15th of July, 1995. Then, again, I don't suppose you expected any less from him. In opening his case, Mr. McCloskey praised Vinko Pandurevic's bravery as a soldier. In concluding the opening of his Defence, I simply say it is a far, far braver thing that he does now than he's ever done before. Thank you. I'll call General Pandurevic to give evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Do you prefer to have the break now, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, we'll do 20, 25 minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. So Mr. Pandurevic to be moved to the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, you are about to start giving evidence. I take it this is a decision you made out of your own choice. You still have a right to go back on your decision, if you so desire. No one can force you to say anything in these proceedings. So if it is still your intention to proceed and give evidence, please make the solemn declaration that you're familiar with, and then we can start.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. Again, the understanding is we'll have the break at 10.30. We can have it at 10.30, and then we will have a 25-minute break, as usual, and then the next session will be over an hour and 30 minutes rather than an hour and 45 minutes -- an hour and 20 minutes, sorry, an hour and 20 minutes, rather than the usual time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what your full name is.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The 25th of June, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Jasik, in the Sokolac municipality, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At present, it is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your father, who we know died a year ago, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: His name was Jovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your mother?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Andja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I think you have several brothers and sisters. Would you, if you can, give us their names and ages in descending order, the oldest first.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: My oldest sister, Koviljka, was born in 1950, then my brother Mirko, born in 1956. I was born in 1959. Nenad, 1965, and Petar, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you been married?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: At the moment, well, only once, but I did get married twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you have any children, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I have three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what ages are they?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Natasa is 22, and I have two twin sons who are both 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where is Natasa now, and what is she doing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Natasa resides in Belgrade, and she's a law student.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the two little boys?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: They also reside in Belgrade, and they're elementary school students.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what did your father do for a living?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: My father was a farmer. He was born in a village, and he spent his whole life there. He was -- farming land, and he raised cattle in a primitive way. We all were born in the same village, and we all worked with the same father -- with our father. From the age of 10, we were all engaged in hard physical labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I went to different schools. Since my village is very small, there was no elementary school there. The elementary school was in the neighbouring village. That's where I finished one grade, and I had to travel 3 kilometres in each direction, and the next three grades I finished in an even more distant village. It took me 6 kilometres to travel there. And then the 5th and 6th and 7th grade, I also finished in a new school. I had to travel 9 kilometres again, 10 kilometres to finish my 8th grade, and finally I finished grammar school in Sokolac, and to do that I had to travel 13 kilometres each direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You're going a little quickly. When you say you travelled to each of those schools, how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The interpreter did not interpret your question fully, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you get to school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you told us the village was small. About how many people lived in Jasik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: There were a total of four houses, ten to fifteen people living in them. The neighbouring village also had three or four houses altogether, and there was a small Muslim hamlet very close to my village. There were some five or six houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the village you lived in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The three villages that I've just mentioned share the common name "Vjetrenik," but they were all different hamlets. Two were Serb hamlets, and one was a Muslim hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what contact did you have with Muslims as a child?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Everyday contacts. We farmed the land, we ploughed the same land. My father's land bordered on the land of our Muslim neighbour. We went to school together, we played football together, we minded the cattle together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about religious celebrations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Serbs celebrate their holidays, their family holidays which they celebrate every year, and it was customary in our village that all of our neighbours attended one person's celebration, and these people obviously included all the Muslim neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you regard them as your friends?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we regarded as our friends. According to our belief, a good neighbour is even more important than a brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How about school; what was the composition of the schools you went to, in ethnic terms?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The first grade that I completed, the peoples were mostly Serbs; only three Muslims. And the next three grades I completed in a Muslim village. There were only three or four Serb students. The rest were Muslims, and our teachers were Muslims also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How were you brought up at home to treat people from other ethnic minorities?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: We cherished neighbourly relations. The only thing that distinguished us was religion, and we knew, as children of six or seven, that the Serbs referred to our Muslim neighbours as Turks, and they referred to us as "vlasi," but this was not derogatory, this was more in religious terms, because we knew that the Islam in Bosnia came from Turkey, and that's why we used the term when we referred to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about the sort of attitudes that were taught at school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know that we lived in a communist system which had an attitude towards religious feelings and beliefs and kept them under a certain control, if not oppression. There was a concept of a brotherhood and unity, which was the main postulate on which the Yugoslav society on which the Yugoslav society rested. There were an attempt -- there were attempts to switch from nations to -- from ethnic affiliations to nations, so there was a melting pot and transfer of ethnic groups into one nation as a whole, the Yugoslav nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how did that contrast with the atmosphere, for example, once the war started?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the concept of fraternity and unity and socialist self-management did not survive the history test, and finally the concept of the unity and fraternity was displaced by armed violence which occurred in the whole territory of the former Yugoslavia. And within that context, one could say that that -- the same former Yugoslavia was a creation that came to be through force, and that's -- and that it was in the same way that it broke apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we come on, please, to your military history. At what age did you enroll for military Academy?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Upon graduating from grammar school, I enrolled in the Military Academy. While I was in the third grade of grammar school, I applied, and I was admitted as the only student from Sokolac, and that's why I received a scholarship. And that was the only opportunity for me to receive higher education, and that's why I enrolled in the Military Academy, because the education there, in that school, was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your mother's view of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: She did not approve. She told me, "Once in a uniform, you will always be in a uniform," which meant that I will always be under a certain degree of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did you spend at the Military Academy?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Four years in total; three years in Belgrade and one year in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Upon graduating from the academy, I became the second lieutenant, and I was sent to serve in Ljubljana in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was you position originally when you arrived in Ljubljana, and what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the duty of platoon commander in the School of Reserve Officers. This was the School of Reserve Officers where officers were trained for the Territorial Defence of Slovenia and the reserve units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you study in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A year into my service in Slovenia, I enrolled in the post-graduate studies at that School of Sociology, Political Sciences and Journalism. Prior to that, I to pass some differential exams, all the differences between the exams that I passed at the Military Academy and all the ones that were required for my new school. I received my Master's degree in 1989, and I became a -- I obtained a Master's degree in Humanities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll just get this out of the way at this stage. I want briefly to put a document into e-court without looking at it. It's P372. We're not going to examine this document in any great detail, General Pandurevic. Do you recognise the document that's on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This is information about myself, as a professional soldier, and this is one of the documents from my personal file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's a document that contains details of your, amongst other things, promotions within the army, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Every professional soldier, or officer, rather, has a personal file which is opened on the day when they start serving, and when they get a rank, and this file is updated throughout their career. This is a picture of their professional career.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, unless anybody objects, I'm going to lead you on the details of your various professions in the army. You told us that you began as a second lieutenant in July of 1982. Were you promoted in July of 1983 to the rank of lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, both is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you then promoted in 1987 to the rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in 1991 to the rank of captain first class?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think on the 7th of January of 1993, you achieved the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on the 23rd of June of 1994, you achieved the rank of lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 31st of December of 1995, you achieved the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on the 28th of June of 1997, you were promoted to the rank of major general in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in March of 2001, you became a General in the Army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Army of Yugoslavia, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now go back to Slovenia, please. At the time you were living in Slovenia, were you active in politics?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I became a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia relatively early, when I was still in grammar school, in the first grade thereof. When I arrived in Ljubljana, I was elected as the president of the youth organisation in my regiment. I was also the secretary of the party organisation of the League of Communists in the Yugoslav People's Army. These were posts that were not paid. However, professionally, I was the president of the Youth Alliance in the Yugoslav People's Army in the Ljubljana Corps, which covered most of Slovenia, excluding the Styria region, from December 1988 to December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have a political function within the army in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: It was a military and political duty. I was the assistant commander for political work and also his assistant. That was the assistant commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you at any time been a member of the SDS or any nationalist political party?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the process of the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the process of dissolution of the League of Communists in Yugoslavia, there was a new party, the Movement for Yugoslavia, and most officers were members of this party. This was an attempt to save and preserve Yugoslavia as it was, and for a brief period of time I was a member of that organisation. However, after that, I was no longer a member of any of the two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us something about the life you established in Slovenia? How long did you live there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Nine years, and I can say that these were the most beautiful years of my life. I was completely integrated into the Slovenian society. I learned the language, I studied. To cut a long story short, I perceived Slovenia as my own country, as my homeland, as my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you have family in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was married in Slovenia. I had a wife and a daughter. I currently don't have a family in Slovenia, but I have a lot of friends and acquaintances. The current prime minister of Slovenia was a junior at the Military Academy, Borut Pahor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you learn to speak Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the composition of the units that you were a member of whilst you were living in Slovenia? Where did your colleagues and superiors and subordinates come from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: When I assumed the duty of the platoon commander of the School of Reserve Officers, that platoon was composed 100 per cent of Slovenians. It was a school that was intended primarily and exclusively for that area. However, the other units within the brigade in which I served were multiethnic of mixed composition. Both soldiers and officers were composed that way. There were Muslims, Croats, Serbs, Slovenians. My battalion commander was a Muslim, Vahid Karavelic, who was later on the commander of the Sarajevo Corps. Tihomir Blaskic worked with me, who was also tried here. I was his company commander, and he was also my best man at my wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We know you wrote certain magazine articles at the time. What were your views on the secession of Slovenia from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: At the time when Slovenia was still in Yugoslavia, the process of the disintegration of Yugoslavia society were taking place, and they were most pronounced in Slovenia, and it was the Youth Organisation of Slovenia that was at the forefront of this movement. I was actually involved in all of their activities. I wrote articles for certain journals and periodical magazines. I contributed to two of them, and it was with the deepest regret that I looked at all these processes that were taking place, and I was saddened by the imminent dissolution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your position when eventually war did break out in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was the assistant for political work of the battalion commander, and I was also his deputy at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what happened when the war started?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The war in Slovenia broke out spontaneously. The units of the JNA were blocked in the barracks. First it was the border crossings that came under attack and also the barracks Boris Kidric in Ljubljana, where I also served. It was blocked by the units of the Territorial Defence of Slovenia. So I found myself as a target of those whom I trained only a year before that. Fortunately enough, the armed conflict did not last long and did not result in a great number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you leave Slovenia, and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In mid-August, the last members of the brigade that I served in left Ljubljana, and we arrived in Zenica. I spent several days in Zenica, and then I returned to Ljubljana to fetch my car and to take my wife with me, and we went to Belgrade. I travelled via Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then I ended up in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a small thing, just one date I think we're missing. But when did the war break out in Slovenia, what month?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was on the 26th of June that the Assembly of Slovenia proclaimed independence, and that was also when the war broke out. It was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You told us then that you went to Belgrade. Why did you go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I had already been admitted as a student at the Command Staff Academy, and my education was supposed to start in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you complete that course?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The education was for two years, and it was continuous education. Unfortunately, I never completed. I had to drop out only a month after I started because of the war that had broken out in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: After the 20 days spent at the school, I was sent to the 19th Mountain Brigade of the Uzice Corps in the territory of Western Serbia. I was appointed as the battalion commander on a temporary basis there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the situation like in that unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The situation was very confusing. The mobilisation that was launched failed, and the army had literally broken up. The commanders were all removed, and us new officers tried to consolidate the brigade and to -- and to start working with it, but it was not easy at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where were you stationed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I spent about a month with the battalion in training on Mount Zlata near Uzice, and then I was sent to the theatre of war in the territory of Dubrovnik and Neretva and Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we take the break now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty-five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before the break, General Pandurevic, we left you at Trebinje. During what period of time were you stationed at Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was stationed in the Trebinje area from the beginning of October up until mid-November 1991, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you there involved in any combat activity?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The unit was sent there to engage in combat, but this was a period of certain truces that were more or less respected, so there was no serious fighting, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where did you go after Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from Trebinje, the unit was disbanded, and I spent about seven days on leave. Then a mobilisation of other units was carried out, and I was designated as battalion commander or, rather, the Chief of Staff of a light infantry brigade that consisted of companies that had been formed anew within the framework of the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long did you hold the position of Chief of Staff within that unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, luckily or unluckily, for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: After the brigade that consisted of companies, there were about six companies in the brigade, six infantry companies, I was designated as the commander of the 1st Infantry Company, because according to the plan for the company, that company was supposed to engage along a separate axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where did you go with that company?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In mid-December 1991, I was sent to the area of Western Slovenia, to the north of Sava River, to the Pokucani [phoen] area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I remained there until around the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, where were you between March 1992 and June of 1992, and what rank and position were you filling?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from Western Slovenia, the very same battalion was mobilised again, the one that I had been sent to the Herzegovina and Dubrovnik battle-field with, and as the commander of that battalion, at the beginning of April I was sent to the Visegrad area. At the time, I had the rank of captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And -- thank you. What was the demographic and military situation that you needed to deal with in the Visegrad area at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that as far as political and demographic conditions are concerned, I was more familiar with them in Croatian and Slovenia than in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, on the basis of the information that I obtained at the time, the situation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was critical. The first armed clashes had already commenced in the Visegrad area. Armed conflict had already started, and most of the Serbian population had left the municipality, whereas the Muslim forces had taken over the hydroelectric centre in Visegrad, and they threatened to flood Visegrad and all other towns downstream along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that the situation when you arrived there with your unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived from the direction of the place called Rudo, which is south-east of Visegrad, I arrived at the hydroelectric power-plant. The Muslim forces were still present there. In the immediate vicinity of the hydroelectric power-plant, there was a military warehouse that belonged to the JNA, and there were about 1.000 Muslim refugees, civilians, who were in that warehouse because they were afraid that the town would be flooded. I went to the hydroelectric plant with my forces. The Muslim forces left the plant and withdrew to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how did events develop in Visegrad while you were there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, in just a few days, peace and order had been established in the municipality of Visegrad. The Muslim and Serbian population returned to the town, over 90 per cent of that population. The Muslims and Serbs formed the government. The JNA was, in fact, the force that was supposed to prevent any further conflicts from breaking out in that area, and they managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a time when negotiations were ongoing as to whether the JNA should remain in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or as to whether they should withdraw to Yugoslavia. Initially, it was said that for the following four years, the JNA would remain in the territory of Bosnia. However, suddenly a decision was taken according to which the JNA should withdraw from Bosnia. So on the 18th of May, together with other elements from the brigade, I withdrew to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you return to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to Visegrad around mid-June or at the beginning of June. I can't exactly remember the date. I relieved myself of the duties of the commander of the battalion, and I arrived in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And had the situation altered by the time you returned there in June?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, while our brigade was preparing to withdraw from Visegrad, the population, both the Serbian and Muslim population, was somewhat unsettled. There was a kind of polarization, a separation of the population on the basis of their villages and settlements. So when I returned to Visegrad, I came across a wartime situation, and demarcation lines or, rather, conflict lines had already been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what sort of units were involved in this wartime situation by the time you got back there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, there were two Visegrad brigades. One was Serbian; the other was Muslim. In addition to them, there were some paramilitary formations that had arrived from Serbia that had been partially formed out of individuals from the local territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What paramilitary groups did you first encounter when you arrived back in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various groups there. Some called themselves the White Eagles. Others just called themselves volunteers. Some were from Priboj, that's the South-Eastern part of Serbia, somewhere from Uzice. Some called themselves Dejanovci, others White Eagles. I don't really know the names of each of the groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when did you first encounter any such unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I came across such units while the JNA unit was still in the area. And after I had returned, I came across those units or such units in town. They were staying in some hotels. They were trying to live the life of luxury and to engage in warfare in a manner that was particular to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how did you deal with it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Since at the beginning I didn't have any direct contact with them, the leadership of the municipality complained to me and said they had certain problems with such units. One morning, I came across a group of such soldiers in the vicinity of the restaurant where food for my soldiers would be prepared. There was a clash between myself and them because I didn't allow them to enter the restaurant to get food from that restaurant. It was a quite intense clash, weapons were pointed, but we managed to calm the situation down. And they requested certain forms of transport so that it would be possible for them to leave Visegrad. I asked the president of the municipality to provide them with such transport, and they then left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And after you returned to Visegrad in June, how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as commander of the Visegrad Brigade, I was there until the 20th of -- 27th of September, 1992. While I acted as the commander of the Visegrad Brigade, there was an oral order from the Main Staff, ordering us to form a tactical group for Gornje Podrinje. It was to consist of five brigades, a brigade from Rogatica, the Visegrad brigade, the Rudo Brigade, the Cajnice Brigade, and the Gorazde Brigade. And such a group was actually formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your command structure in that time in June to December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: From June to the end of December, I was the commander of the Visegrad Brigade; at the same time, the Chief of Staff of the tactical group from the time of its formation. And after the commander of the Rudo Brigade was killed, he was killed by Serbian soldiers, I took over the command of the Visegrad Tactical Group. And from the 27th of September, my command post was in the town of Rudo. Sometime in November, an order was issued according to which the Gorazde Brigade was to be reorganised. It was also part of the tactical group, but it was falling apart because the population had been expelled from the Gorazde area, and I was ordered to form that brigade, to be the commander of the Gorazde Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have a corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The situation was particular. The Visegrad area was very isolated, in geographical terms and in terms of command relationships. We just had a telephone link to the Main Staff and telephone links between the brigades. Up until November, until the time that the Drina Corps was established, that area was not organised very well, in military terms. It was only when the Drina Corps was formed in November that all these units became part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what, physically, did your command amount to in Rudo?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The command was located in the cultural centre or the centre of the 1st Proletarian Brigades that was established 1941, the 22nd of December; that was also the day of the JNA. In addition to myself, in the brigade command, there was a reserve major, an operations officer. There was a reserve lieutenant. There was a liaison officer, and there was a -- or, rather, communications officer, and there was a typist, no one else, a woman who was a typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how were you in contact with the brigade or brigades?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I established contact with the brigades by telephone, using reserve post office telephones, ordinary telephones. I didn't have an encrypted teleprinter, so I could only establish contact through the Drina Corps once it had been established. I could only establish such contact through the Drina Corps after it had been established, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want you to analyse for us a document. Can we have 7D728 into e-court, please. Now, this document in English has the title "Combat Order," and appears to be a document signed by you. And the 10th of November, 1992, was that a date before or after the establishment of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This date is subsequent to the establishment of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you help us as to what this order reflects in the history of events in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This order concerns a warning to the units of tactical groups about the possible enemy activity at the time planned for an exchange of the dead between the Visegrad Brigade and the Muslim Visegrad Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just very briefly, can we have a look at 7D742. And I'm told I have to make sure that the complete version is called into e-court. It's a two-page document, General Pandurevic. Please tell us if you want to digest both pages before I move to my questions.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Could I see the other page, the second page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. We've only just started to deal with documents, General Pandurevic. We're going to deal with a lot during the course of the next few days. We do have them all here in a hard copy, so if there's any document you wish to look at in hard copy, we will provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a document dated the 21st of November of 1992. What event or events does that reflect in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This document doesn't concern Visegrad. It concerns the Gorazde Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: As I, as commander of the tactical group, was mainly engaged in establishing or reorganising the Gorazde Brigade, I had moved closer to Visegrad, to a place called Vardiste. And the command post for this brigade had been -- was supposed to be located there because it had been completely broken up. All the population had withdrawn from the area of Gorazde and moved over to Serbia. It was necessary to bring those people back to reorganise the brigade and to send it into action. This order shows that the corps commander decided to appoint me as commander of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long were you engaged in that task?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was very serious about the task. I started establishing the brigade. I found buildings for their accommodation, buildings to keep equipment in, and after a month an order was issued for me to report to Zvornik, although I had barely taken over the duties I've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you first come to learn of your -- of the requirement that you should go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, one day Lieutenant-Colonel Ugljanin came to Vardiste. He was the chief of security in the Drina Corps, and he relayed an order from the corps commander to me, and I think it was Colonel Zivanovic at the time, an order according to which I was to report to Zvornik, and I was to be a brigade commander in Zvornik. I was completely taken aback by this, as well as other people in the command of the Gorazde Brigade. They had developed good relationships with me, we were on very good terms, and they expected me to remain there, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Zvornik before?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I had passed through Zvornik before on my way from Sokolac to Belgrade. However, I never stayed in Zvornik, and I wasn't very familiar with the situation in Zvornik, or I knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So did you go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Zvornik. I was driven there by an escort. I arrived at the command post of the Zvornik Brigade. At the time in December 1992, the post was located in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you formally resign your position in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this was contrary to all the military rules and regulations. I quite simply bid farewell to those people from the brigade and left, on the basis of the oral order from the Drina Corps command. I didn't transfer my duties to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was the first person you met when you got to the Command of the Zvornik Brigade in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, together with Lieutenant-Colonel Puljanin [phoen] to the building where the command was located, I met Captain First Class Mijo Dragutinovic. That's how he introduced himself. I had never seen him before. Lieutenant-Colonel Ugljanin said, "This is your new commander," and then he turned around and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could we have a quick look, please, at P417. It's point 60 at which is page 18 in the English and page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat for the transcript the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. P417.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, these are the provisional service regulations of the Army of Republika Srpska of August 1992, and point 60 describes the procedure for the hand-over of duties by a commanding officer. You've already told us what happened when you left your previous position. Did anything such as is described in point 60 happen when you arrived in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Bullet point 60 of the regulations speaks about the hand-over of duties from the level of the squad commander to the brigade commanders. Nothing of the sort as described in bullet point 60 happened when it comes to my arrival in Zvornik. Truth be told, there was a war going on, and one could not expect that everything mentioned in the bullet point could be carried out or honoured. In any case, a minimum should have been done. The brigade command should have been all in one place. The corps commander should have been present there, and also the person who had been acting as brigade commander should have been there, and there should have been a meeting, a briefing and debriefing, and I should have been put abreast of the overall situation in the Zvornik Brigade. However, none of this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Probably my fault, General Pandurevic, but the one thing I don't think you've told us yet is what the precise date was that you arrived in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Zvornik on the 18th of December, 1992. I remember, because the following day is St. Nicholas day, the patron saint. That I remember. And I also remember one more thing. When I heard initial information about the situation in the Zvornik Brigade, I told the driver who brought me from Visegrad not to leave, to stay put just for a little while longer, because I might be inclined to join him on his journey back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was the acting commander of the Zvornik Brigade on the 18th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I wasn't clear, to be honest. The former brigade commander who had been appointed on an order was Dragan Petkovic. He was seriously wounded in October, and he was undergoing treatment at the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. My impression was that the duties of the brigade commander were discharged by Dragan Obrenovic. However, there was a lieutenant-colonel there, Bosancic, who according to some information that I received from the command, acted on behalf of the commander, and it was his own decision to say to Obrenovic, "Obrenovic, you are now going to be carrying out the duties." There was no paper to show clearly who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you meet Dragan Obrenovic on the day of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime late in the afternoon, Dragan Obrenovic returned to the command of the brigade from the field. I introduced myself to him, we met. I'd never seen him before. I didn't even know that that man existed. In the brief outlines, he briefed me on the situation in the brigade. And as of that moment on, pursuant to an oral order of the corps commander, I de facto assumed the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I just want very briefly to look at some combat reports from that particular period of time. And can we start, please, by, in e-court, having 7D731. This is the regular report of the 18th of December of 1992. It appears to have been signed by Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you were shown a report for the day or offered the opportunity to sign a combat report on the day you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand this document, this is a report which was drafted pursuant to an order of the Drina Corps command and sent to the Drina Corps command as well, and it speaks of the current deployment of the units of the Zvornik Brigade. I did not see the document at the time, and I didn't sign it either. I was not even aware of it, its existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we come on to 7D740.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is the regular combat report for the following day, the day after you arrived in Zvornik, the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a regular combat report dated 19 December. I was in the Command, and that was the first day -- or if you take that I was there on the 18th as well, then it would have been the second day of my command of the Zvornik Brigade. I can see that the person who was supposed to sign it was Chief of Staff Captain Dragan Obrenovic. It may be that the duty officer didn't know that I was there, or maybe he did it by sheer automatism. He just continued putting Dragan Obrenovic's name in lieu of the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly in this succession of documents, 7D741. And I think the document in Serbian needs to be moved up just a little bit. Thank you. This is the regular combat report for the 20th of December, and was that the first report signed by you as commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In light of the fact that during that period of time there were two combat reports drafted during the day, one around 12.00 noon or -- and the other in the course of the afternoon, around 1700 or 1800 hours, one of them was signed by me, and that's the report that you see in front of you. Whether I signed the first one as well, I don't know. It may well be the case, or maybe not. In any case, this was done on the 20th of December, the day when I actually started signing my combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just wonder whether we can take a moment to recap at this stage. On the 18th of December, 1992, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In June 1992, I was 33, which means that I was 33 and a half years old in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what rank did you hold within the army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've told us you previously commanded a brigade. For how long had you done that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: For around six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And apart from the five or six days you told us about, had you ever been a Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And had you ever attended command staff school?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I started attending command staff school. I spent there 20 days, never completed it. And this is the school without which you would not qualify for the rank of colonel, and you could not be brigade commander. However, after I completed my Master's degree, my establishment specialty was altered, so that subsequently I no longer needed the completed school as a requirement, although I was sent again in September 1993 to the school. However, this referral was not approved by the Command of the Drina Corps because of the war operations, and I never went back to that school, whereas my -- the rest of my generation that also dropped out of the school at the same time as I did continued that education after the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we complete the full picture, what experience had you had by that stage as the commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: My experience was rather modest, both as battalion commander in peacetime -- I did not have any, to be honest, because all I had as battalion commander was spent in wartime. I had some experience, but only six months, which was not enough for me to assume the duties of brigade commander and act as an experienced officer in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: According to the rules of the JNA, what rank and experience ought you to have had to command a brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The procedure in the JNA required for somebody to become brigade commander to have been battalion commander for at least two or three years, and then the operations officer in the brigade, but not necessarily, but the Chief of Staff in the brigade, and he should have had the rank of lieutenant-colonel or colonel and should have been about 45 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I recall seeing a document about maybe five minutes ago or so, in which there was a description of how the recommendation that your client be appointed as brigade commander was being endorsed, but it was not approved or no approval had yet been forthcoming. What I would like to know is: How come the recommendation itself was endorsed if your client is now explaining to us that the criteria would have been somewhat different and whether he has knowledge that the decision to approve his appointment as brigade commander was withheld at the time because of what he's just described to us now; namely, that certain requirements had to have been met? I don't know if I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I know the document and I know to what it refers, and I'm absolutely confident General Pandurevic will as well and will give you the explanation you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think if I haven't been clear enough, then we can perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sure you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, you heard the President's inquiry. Can you deal with that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a document. I don't know whether it is on the list or not, and in this document Lieutenant-Colonel Cerevic, who at the time was a member of the commander of the Drina Corps, sent a proposal to the commander of the Drina Corps for me to be the commander of the Gorazde Brigade. Immediately after that, an order was issued by General Mladic about my appointment to that position.
