That letter document also exists; I don't whether it is in e-court, whether it can be seen now or not. However, that was the procedure, and that's how things went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in terms of the document that suggests that there was a period of time when authority was withheld, was that for a very long period of time or not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what time-period you're referring to. However, at that time the appointments and the -- were not accompanied by adequate documents and orders. People would first be referred to -- referred to certain duties and positions, and written documents would follow that. In order for somebody to be appointed as the brigade commander, the person in charge of that appointment was the minister of defence, nobody else, and only the corps commander or the commander of the Main Staff could move for that position or propose that person for that position and appoint them temporarily. There were periods of interruptions in the formal drafting of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, if we need to return to that, what we can do, but I hope that deals with your inquiry. If it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's move ahead, let's move ahead. My question was more related to whether, in spite of requirements and regulations, in reality, appointments as to brigade commanders were being made when there was reason to believe that the requirements weren't there. Yes, I see Ms. Fauveau standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there's a mistake; not a very significant one. But before I let my colleague continue, on page 45, line 18 and 19 and 20 of the transcript, one reads "Lieutenant-Colonel Cerevic ..." [In English] "...of the Drina Corps sent a proposal to the commander of the Drina Corps." [Interpretation] I think there was a mistake in the translation, so if the witness could please confirm the position of Colonel Cerevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good point, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a transcript issue. There may be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did you actually say? You understand English from what we saw from another document. So page 45, lines 18, 19, and 20, 21. What would you correct there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was Lieutenant-Colonel Cerevic the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, Lieutenant-Colonel Cerevic was the assistant for morale in the Drina Corps, and the corps commander at the time was Colonel Zivanovic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we're all happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And while we are at this, on line 23 on the same page, was it General Panic or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about General Mladic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm raising it, because I heard you say "General Mladic," but we have "Panic" here. Okay, let's continue, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like you just to briefly look, if you would, at the manual for the work of command and staff, point 27. That's P699 in e-court, page 20 in the English and pages 21 and 22 in B/C/S. And, in particular, the aspect of that point, which says: "It is necessary for the officers in commands and staffs to have previous experience in exercising control in those activities and units whose interests they represent in performing their particular function in the command." We'll come on to the numbers of professional officers in the Zvornik Brigade in due course, but you had an opportunity to assess the experience of your officers in command and staff. What sort of previous experience had they had?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In any case, they did not have the experience -- the experience envisaged by bullet point 27 of this instruction for the work of commands and staffs. And particularly in combat campaigns, one requires a lot of experience and knowledge. The officers who were members of the Zvornik Brigade Command were mostly reserve officers who had previously been members of the staffs of Territorial Defence, at much higher -- lower positions than the ones that they were appointed to in the Zvornik Brigade. And I'm also including here Dragan Obrenovic as the Chief of Staff and myself as the brigade commander. I feel the need to explain to the Trial Chamber, and especially the President of the Trial Chamber, in regard to the previous question and answer, it is true that there were criteria that somebody had to meet in order to be appointed to a certain position. What happened in the war was that one commander of the Zvornik Brigade was a lieutenant-colonel, another one as well, and the third one was also lieutenant-colonel. They offered several colonels to us in the duty. However, they were experienced enough to know what this meant. And finally, it was I who was put in that position, not even suspected -- suspecting what lies ahead of me. I assumed the position without meeting the necessary requirements for the post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, moving on from there, you've told us that the previous commander of the Zvornik Brigade was a man called Dragan Petkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at the time you arrived in Zvornik, you were aware that he had been injured in 1992, in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Following on from what you've just said, were you familiar with what rank he held?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I knew that he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'd like us, please, to look at a document we first put into e-court, your service record. That's P372, and we need to look at page 4 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S, please. And very briefly, General Pandurevic, what is that? What does that page in your service record record?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: What I see in front of me on the screen is an order issued by the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska on the appointment of Vinko Pandurevic as the commander of the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. The date is 8 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we go to another page in that document. That's page 8 in English, and page 16 in the B/C/S. And what does that page of your service record indicate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This document originates or is in reference to the previous document. This is a report on the take-over of duty pursuant to the order of the minister of defence. I was appointed as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and I assumed the duty officially on the 26th of October, 1993. This was done formally. Everything was done on that day, although it says here that I reported to the unit on the 13th of December. This is not correct because I reported to the unit on the 18th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, between the 18th of December, 1992, and the 26th of October, 1993, did you regard yourself as being in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was in command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So what was the effect of an order formally appointing you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This order regulated my status in the service. As of this order onwards, I started receiving salary. My files were updated based on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Now, what was the state of the brigade when you arrived there in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and be very brief when describing the situation as it was. Based on the reports that I received on the 18th and the briefing that I received on the 18th when I arrived in Zvornik, it was said to this Trial Chamber previously that on the 6th or 7th November, a lot of civilians and soldiers were killed in the territory of Glodjansko Brdo and that one battalion of the Zvornik Brigade was completely dissolved, and that battalion withdrew to the outskirts of the town of Zvornik. Another battalion was in the area of Drinjaca, south of Zvornik, some 12 kilometres further away, and it was completely encircled. The territory between Crni Vrh and Nemici [phoen], which is north-west of the city of Zvornik, was not covered by the Serb forces, which means that territory was completely empty. The other battalions were in very dire straits. The commander of these battalions were next to impossible. When I heard all that, I wanted to return to Visegrad. I did not want to resume the duty of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. However, as a person who sincerely and militarily understood any order, I took the job, and I embarked on a very difficult mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you know how many soldiers there were in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was first asked about the strength. None was able to provide me with an exact figure. They said between 5.600 up until 6.000 odd. It's necessary to make a distinction between the number of people in the brigade and the number of soldiers. When I say that, what I have in mind is how many of those people are prepared to carry out combat tasks as soldiers. The brigade was organised, as far as I can remember, into about 11 infantry battalions. Their strength was more than the strength of the battalions in July, or the strength was different with respect to the battalions in July, so I wouldn't want to mention any figures in order to avoid creating confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've told us that at the time you arrived, the command of the brigade was in Orahovac. In strategic terms, where was that in relation to combat?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the brigade command was practically at the first front-line. That's contrary to tactical rules. However, the corps command took such a decision because they knew that this territory was under threat, and if they placed the brigade command there, then some of the units that secured the command of the brigade would be in the area, present in the area, and would thus be able to provide a minimum form of protection there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want us to look at a few contemporaneous reports to get a flavour of the situation, and we'll look, please, at 7D946, a regular combat report for the 19th of December. And we need to look at page 6 in the B/C/S, please. When you've had the chance to refresh your memory of the document, I wonder if you could let us know, insofar as you already haven't, what state of affairs that is describing.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Here we have the partial description of the overall situation in the territory of the Zvornik Brigade in December 1992. We can see that all the Serbian villages weren't protected or they were poorly protected. Enemy forces succeeded in entering the village of Grujici, they succeeded in looting and killing some older women, and Serbian forces were not very strong and put up minimum resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we go to P280, please. This is an order about a month after you arrived in January of 1993. Does this reflect the combat situation and the state of the brigade there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll up a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted on the basis of the way events developed in the area at the time and on the basis of the intelligence and information that we had, and this information concerns the purposes of the enemy. I issued an order to units of the Zvornik Brigade, saying that they should defend all inhabited places and the town of Zvornik at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think you might like to look at the second page, and paragraph 2 in particular, and give us some comments on how that reflects the capabilities and alertness of the troops at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Item 2 mentions how the Zvornik Brigade units should act, how they had been acting, and it states that they had acted in an inadequate and inefficient manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on another month to 7D470, please, 470. And perhaps you can tell us what event this described.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report dated the 18th of February, 1993. It's similar to standard combat reports. Item 1 mentions enemy activity, and it's mortar fire on the Kiseljak inhabited area. The second part mentions the exhumation of soldiers who were killed in Glodjansko Brdo, and the mentions Kamenica. The date was the 6th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And following on from the reference to Glodjansko Brdo, can we have a look, please, at 7D1007, and in particular paragraph 2 here.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This item is about the exhumation and identification, burial, of a certain number of soldiers who were killed at Kamenica. The figure is mentioned 35, and two were unidentified. Rather, the figure of 22 soldiers relates to identified soldiers. I apologise. I remember that funeral. I attended it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: During your association with the Zvornik Brigade, was there ever a larger massacre of your men than the events at Glodjansko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, what we have been discussing is, in fact, the massacre Glodjansko Brdo. As far as I can remember, we have already seen photographs that -- photographs of the event. And on the 7th of January, 1993, there was a massacre in the village of Kravica. I, with some forces from the Zvornik Brigade, was involved in preventing the Muslim forces from advancing any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I was simply interested in the number of members of the brigade that were lost at Glodjansko Brdo. You've read a document now showing there was 35. Was there ever any single incident of combat where you lost more than 35 men?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This is the number of men found. According to other information from the time, there were other men who were listed as missing. There were other men from the Sekovici Brigade, but this is the largest number of soldiers killed in one day from the Zvornik Brigade. That was the case for the entire wartime period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in seeking to improve standards in the brigade, did the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska embark upon a survey of the brigades in 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff, from the time it was established, was in a very difficult situation when it comes to controlling or establishing control over the territory of Republika Srpska and when it comes to organising the army. Since the Main Staff didn't have many professional officers, it wasn't very numerous, it had a difficult task. However, the Main Staff did send special teams of officers into the field. They visited the brigades, the corps, and examined the combat readiness or tried to assess their combat readiness. They also visited the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you ever see an assessment of the Zvornik Brigade by the Main Staff at about that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see an assessment of its combat readiness. It was the Main Staff that made such an assessment, I think, in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In general terms, what was that assessment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the assessment of combat readiness is carried out in a standard manner, and there were positive and negative experiences, but there were more negative experiences and decisions. The general assessment was that the Zvornik Brigade was cumbersome, that the commander wasn't in a position to successfully command such a brigade, it would be necessary to divide the brigade into two parts. And I think its assessment was not as good as the assessment given to the Bratunac and Sekovici Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The document's still, unfortunately, in translation, so we may need your help a little bit, General Pandurevic, but the document is 7D1001. And I wonder if you could, a good deal less quickly than you have been speaking so far, just read, as it were, the contents of that cover sheet for us.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: "The Main Staff of the VRS, strictly confidential number, the 5th of March, 1993. "Assessment of combat ready of units in the Drina Corps," being forwarded to the commander of the Drina Corps: "We hereby attach to this an assessment of combat readiness in some of your units. Examine this assessment, draw up a plan to deal with any shortcomings, and include these objectives in your working plans. "General Ratko Mladic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we now go to page 5, please. We can see there the Zvornik Brigade has a number. Is that the score it achieved?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade was given the score 3.20, in brackets "fair."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And going down to paragraph (b), to the bottom of that page, I wonder if you could read for us the conclusions there, please.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: "Weaknesses and shortcomings. "The brigade is composed of ten infantry battalions. If we add support units and other elements to this, then it is quite clear that its composition is too cumbersome, and even a far stronger command would not be able to ensure adequate command and control. Documentation at the level of the battalion command isn't provided by daily command and control. The firing system at the level of the battalion hasn't been professionally organised. The firing possibilities -- the firing equipment possibilities haven't been made adequate use of. There is a noticeable lack of professional and qualified officers at all levels of command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to the score, did any brigade score lower than the Zvornik Brigade in this assessment of combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I think that this document also mentions the Bratunac and 1st Bircani or, rather, Sekovici Brigades. As far as I can remember, their assessments were more favourable than the assessments of the Zvornik Brigade. If we could have a look at the entire document, I would then be able to state something with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that may mean that this is an appropriate moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, I was just going to suggest that. Twenty-five minutes from now, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the question I asked you just before the break was probably a little ahead of myself. I wonder if we could go, in the document that is on the screen in e-court, to page 6, please. And you've now got a hard copy of the document, and there are some further comments there. About halfway down the first paragraph, I can see the Serbian word "Prisutan." I wonder if you could read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you like this, but during the break we were informed that Mr. Ostojic's client, that's Mr. Beara, wasn't feeling well, and I authorised his return to the detention centre. I apologise to my colleagues for not informing them before we came into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope it's nothing to do with Mr. Ostojic's return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, would you read the comment slowly for us that begin with the word "Prisutan." It's on page 6, and I know you now have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Let me just find the word, "Prisutan." Yes, I found it now. "Something is present," in inverted commas, "someone else will do that." I don't know if it's necessary to explain what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know what it means?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the usual phrase used in the territory of Yugoslavia. One could say my concerns can be transferred to someone else. That means if I don't do it, someone else will, so it's just a matter of letting someone else carry out one's duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the Main Staff reporting? How did that phrase relate to the Zvornik Brigade at the time they assessed it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, this has to do with the lack of motivation of soldiers and officers when it came to carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I want to look briefly, please, at page 14, at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I wonder if you could just read us slowly the last paragraph of that page.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: "In the brigade, military subordination from detachments to brigade commands is not yet fully functional. Soldiers and officers have demonstrated a considerable amount of willfulness and also the desire to lead on the basis of their own decisions. This creates a certain amount of confusion when it comes to organising the daily life and work of the units and when it comes to establishing relationships with third parties. Everyone addresses or turns to the brigade command for the slightest things."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, given that we're talking, obviously, about March of 1993, the comments that were made about the Zvornik Brigade, were they comments that you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: After the Zvornik Brigade had been controlled and visited in March, the team had a meeting with me in the brigade command, and they told us, in rough terms, about the assessment of the situation, and then this report followed. I was familiar with the situation at the time, and I agreed with the assessment. Perhaps with regard to page 17, I would add a general conclusion. It says: "Establish a tactical group consisting of three brigades and appoint a more experienced officer as commander of the tactical group." So the Zvornik Brigade was equivalent to three light infantry brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the course of our last break, you had the opportunity to go through a hard copy of the document. Did any brigade score a lower mark than the Zvornik Brigade in this Main Staff assessment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No. Apart from the Zvornik Brigade, the Bratunac Brigade was assessed, as well as the Bircani and the Sekovici Brigades. The Bircani and Sekovici Brigade was given a score, 3.35. And the Bratunac Brigade -- just a minute, I think it was 3.35, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move off that Brigade, I do apologise for the fact it's untranslated, but I have to say in our defence, it was submitted for translation five months ago, but as yet it hasn't come back translated. I'll let you know when it has. Now, General Pandurevic, we've looked at, as it were, your position, the position of your officers, the general position in the brigade. Let's move on to your own personal perception a bit. What were the problems with commanding and controlling the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few problems. There's no doubt about that. Every brigade has a way in which it's organised and established. This is the idea one has about the brigade. It has to do with what is set forth in the rules, but its dynamic structure represents another element, and this has to do with how it functions in concrete situations. So when we tried to apply the idea as to how it should function in practice, we had problems. In order to establish control over all the units in the Zvornik Brigade, it was essential for me to have the aid of all my subordinate officers and of all my associates. I tried to find the best way of organising the brigade, given the strength of the brigade. I tried to establish the best possible links between myself and subordinate units, but to verify the actual situation and to assess the actual situation, I would have had to be present in the field; I would have had to be present at the front-line; I would have had to mingle with the soldiers because this is the only way you can gain a real insight into the situation, and it's the best way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many of the battalion commanders were professional soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The battalion commanders were usually foot soldiers with some more courage than others, or reserve officers. The commander of the 3rd Battalion, for example, in July 1995, was a professional officer, Branko Studen, and the commander of the Mixed Artillery Division, Captain Milos Maksimovic. They were the only two professional officers. The others were either foot soldiers or reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about the brigade, generally; how many professional officers were there in the whole of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The number changed in the course of the war. However, it was a very small percentage at all times. I believe that it was anything between 10 and 15 per cent [as interpreted], when it comes to the professional officers in the brigade, in comparison with the total figure of 270 officers that one professional brigade is supposed to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you say 10 and 15 per cent or something else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, I said 10 to 15 men, officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did the battalion soldiers come from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The battalion soldiers came from the villages and settlements where these battalions were deployed. At the very beginning of the war, the front-lines were established in the vicinity of the settlements and villages. However, in the Zvornik Brigade there was also one battalion composed of the soldiers whose families had fled from Central Bosnia, and there were also several companies within the other battalions composed of the soldiers who had fled from some other territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how were they equipped?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Since I joined from the Yugoslav People's Army, which had complete armament and equipment and all the necessary materiel and equipment for its soldiers, I was taken by surprise to see the situation as it was in Zvornik. The soldiers had uniforms which did not match. Nobody had a hat or a helmet. They had their personal weapons, but the soldiers were not autonomous. If you, for example, bear in mind the NATO soldier who carries over 30 kilos of equipment to be autonomous, our soldier did not have anything, was very much tied to his own home. He was not well equipped, and he was really badly disposed to carry out any combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What percentage of the battalion soldiers were reservists?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Save for that one battalion commander who was a professional, all the others were reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wasn't merely asking about the commanders. I was asking about, as it were, the whole force. How many soldiers in the battalions were reservists?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: All the foot soldiers in the Zvornik Brigade were reservists. There were no conscripts, there were no professional soldiers, as such; maybe one or two who happened to be there. However, 99 per cent of the force were reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how were the positions kept manned? Was there a system of rotation or what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, there was a system in the Army of Republika Srpska that was called "rotation warring," which originated in the concept of a weekend warrior or weekend soldier. 50 per cent of the soldiers were on positions, and 50 per cent were on furlough, on leave. This was necessary because the soldiers and their families would not have been able to survive otherwise, if any other system was in place. Only in exceptional cases, when the territory was at a particular risk, there would be 70 per cent of the soldiers on the front-line, and only really they, exceptionally a full force, 100 per cent, were on the front-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what authority did you have over those reserve soldiers who were not on duty?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: In compliance with the law on the military, officers, commissioned officers, officers on contract, conscripts, and reserve soldiers on duty are taken as soldiers. In that sense, all those who were on duty were under my jurisdiction. Reserve soldiers who were on leave or were working from home or in their companies were not under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, since you mention that provision, we'll just have a look at it. Can we have a look at P703, please, Article 3. That's B/C/S page 187, and English page 1. Is Article 3 the provision you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the article that I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. What was their attitude to fighting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, nobody wants to fight. In a fight, you can lose your life. All these people appeared to be very emotional because they were defending their families, their homes, and themselves. They still were forced to be engaged. They did not do it really willingly. They had to fight, but not willingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that it was necessary for you to be with them in the battalions on the front-line. Was that possible, for you to do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The basic principle or, rather, the basic relationship in the army is the command relationship. At the level of the brigade, these relationships are not personal, which means that the brigade commander communicates with his subordinates via written orders, which means I would issue written orders to the battalion commanders, and they would then implement such orders. However, when my written order arrived in the battalion command, it was implemented to the extent to which it was acceptable to those to which it referred. The battalion commanders would report back to me that they did whatever they could, and in order for such an order to be implemented fully, it was necessary for me to appear on the spot, in person, and this is what I very often did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever suffer any particular instances of rebellion or mutiny?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: There were all sorts of situations. Before the war, the Army of Republika Srpska did not exist. There was no mobilisation plan. Nobody knew if they would be mobilised into military units or if they would have work obligation. And then the soldiers believed that those who were not in the army did not have a justified reason not to be in the army, and they would often discuss, if John was with them, why Peter wasn't with them as well. So in order to have my orders carried out, I would often conflict with my subordinates. All this should not have happened. A commander should never conflict with his subordinates, but it did happen on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever find yourself in danger?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, although I did not consider that as a danger that would put my life at risk; at least I did not show it. On one occasion sometime in mid-January 1993, I hit a barricade on the road when entering a village. There was a tractor on the road with a machine-gun mounted on it. They prevented me from getting into the village because I had demanded for the men from that village to go to the positions. After a lot of discussion, they dispersed, but they still did not go to the positions. There was a similar situation in 1994 as well, when a company from the village of Skocic, not wanting to alter their defence sector, encircled me, demanding for me to grant them the approval to stay put in the place where they were. I had to give in momentarily, but later on I moved that company gradually. There were cases when whole battalions had to be moved from one defence sector to a different defence sector. It was a painstaking job, and I often had to negotiate for hours with the soldiers of those battalions. However, due to my good negotiation skills, I would succeed. I would not employ my military skills. I'd would rather employ my people-management and psychological skills in order to do such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. There's just one little discreet error I want to deal with. Can we have a look at 7D1046, please. And forgive me, it's page 3 in the English, pages 2 and 3 in the Serbian text. What power or authority did you have to mobilise men to fight?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any powers to mobilise people or to engage materiel and equipment for a fight. There was a law in place, a law -- the law on defence, which regulated those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, sir, if you did need, what procedure would you have to adopt through your staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I was duty bound to contact organs for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs within the staff and send my request to the corps command, and they, in their turn, would contact the minister of defence, asking them to mobilise men or requisition material or technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving away from that, could we please have P2509 placed into e-court. General Pandurevic, are you familiar with this document, which describes the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility for combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: To be very honest, when I was in Zvornik, I did not see this document in this form. I only saw it here. However, I still had to comply with the provisions contained in this document, because they were already in effect when I arrived in Zvornik, and I know what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't want to take too long with this, because I took rather a long time with another witness a long time ago doing this, but I want to see if we can graphically appreciate what this document means. And behind you there's a map. I think you've been provided with a light pen. 7D1056 is the synopsis sheet of the map, and the title in English is: "Responsibility of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade according to the Drina Corps command order of 1992." I wonder if you could, first of all, show us on the map with the light pen where, as it were, what is described in paragraph 1(a) of that order is drawn on this map.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to say something before I proceed, if I may. I'd like to go from the more general things to the more specialised things. In the theory of the war doctrine which we learned in the School of National Defence, there is a term "theatre of war," and this is the entire territory of the state which is engaged in war, and this theatre of war is divided into small rooms, as it were, which are called "front-lines." And below the front-lines for the tactic-group-level units, we have zones. The Army of Republika Srpska was responsible for the theatre of war which was the entire territory of Republika Srpska. The corps, as operative levels, were responsible for the parts of the territory of the Republika Srpska which would be called "front-lines," and within the corps every brigade had its part of the area of responsibility of the corps, and they were called "zones." So the Zvornik Brigade was also given its zone of responsibility for combat operations. This would be its full name, its full identifier, as it were. What does it mean? In practice, this means that the unit which is in charge of a certain area or zone of responsibility for combat operations, since its purpose is to be engaged in combat operations, this unit is responsible for engaging with all the enemy units that appear in that zone or which are in that zone already. And now I'm going to proceed and show you the borders of the zone of responsibility for combat operations of the Zvornik Brigade. We can see this red line, thick line, which I'm showing with not very well visible pen. These are the borders of the zone of responsibility for combat operations of the Zvornik Brigade. As one can see, this zone of responsibility [indicates] extends far beyond the front-line of the enemy side, and it is not only the territory which is under the control of the VRS, but also a territory which is outside that zone. Hence, the Zvornik Brigade was duty-bound, in case of any enemy forces appearing in this zone, to engage in combat with them. Since the Zvornik Brigade was intended for combat operations rather than for training, transport or commercial purposes, it was only responsible for combat operations and nothing else in that zone of combat operations. I apologise for my lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, don't apologise. The area to the west of the front-line, but within the dotted red and yellow line, that was ever within, as it were, the control of the Zvornik Brigade during the period of your command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and what I'm showing now [indicates], this was all my zone of responsibility for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But did you ever occupy any of that territory, the brigade? Did it ever occupy any of that land to the west of the front-line?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The north-west part of the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade never suffered any changes from its very establishment in June 1992. Those were the defence lines along the Serbian settlements, for the most part. There were some minor corrections of movements extending 400 metres. In the southern part, there were some changes to the front-line, and the positions of the Zvornik Brigade were indeed moved. Within this zone of responsibility for combat operations, the Zvornik Brigade had its zone of defence where the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The positions of the battalions are marked on the map. Probably we will need you to indicate where they are, very briefly. Where was the command post of the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I just said that the numbers of the battalions, dating back to 1992 and 1993, differed to the numbers that they had in July 1995. The 1st Battalion was in this territory here [indicates] that was between Malecici [phoen] and Vitinica. And we know that in 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. With my naked eye, I could see the witness pointing to a particular location on the map, but the transmission -- the video transmission was not focussing on that location at the time. If you could kindly point again to the same place, Mr. Pandurevic, please, and the technical troupe please focus on where he is pointing. Thank you. If we have the same map or parts -- relevant parts of it in e-court that he can mark on, then it would perhaps be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic has actually drawn my attention to something that's rather more significant, which is that this map shows the positions of the battalions in 1992, and, frankly, I don't think that's going to be of much interest to you, so I'm going to move away from this map, and perhaps we'll deal with the positions of the battalions in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we've dealt with, as it were, general forces of the Zvornik Brigade. I want to move on to one specific battalion, which is the Manoeuvres Battalion. Did the Manoeuvres Battalion exist as such in December of 1992 when you arrived at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was there anything like it there when you got there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: There was a unit of some 30 men, approximately, which was known as the Scouts -- Scouting and Reconnoitering Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to have a look very quickly at two documents. 7D1089, please. I'm told that the English version of this document is, unfortunately, not in e-court. We'll see if we can correct that overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you'll need to look at paragraph 4, Commander -- General Pandurevic. This is a Main Staff order of the 20th of September of 1993, and paragraph 4 reads: "The Motorised Battalion of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade shall remain in the organisation establishment of this unit, but continue to break it as a manoeuvre unit of the Drina Corps command under the direct command of the Drina Corps. Battalion must manned at 100 per cent of the personnel and material establishment, and shall be considered a completed battalion that may be strengthened with platoons or companies from the Armoured Mechanised Unit." What did that order effectively create?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to correct you. This is an order from the command of the Drina Corps. It's based on an order from the Main Staff. The purpose of this order is to raise the level of combat readiness within the Drina Corps, and this was to be done by forming manoeuvre units that would be capable of engaging in combat outside of their territory, in the place where they had been established. Since the Zvornik Brigade was fairly strong, and since initially it had this Sabotage and Reconnaissance Detachment manned by young soldiers, the corps command decided that that unit or, rather, the strength of the unit, should be increased. It should be formed as a battalion which would be part of the Zvornik Brigade, and it would be under the immediate command or, rather, direct command of the corps. This sounds a little contradictory. It was part of the Zvornik Brigade when it was necessary to provide it with food, clothing and footwear, but when it was necessary to engage in combat, it did so on the basis of orders from the corps. When it came to combat, I could only use it in the zone of responsibility of my brigade. Outside that defence zone of responsibility, I didn't have the right to use them for such purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you allowed to use them of right, or did you have to seek permission to use them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: As I have said, in my brigade's zone of responsibility, especially when urgent action was required, I could act on my own initiative, but if I were to send it outside the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, it was necessary to have an order issued from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to look at a couple of examples of how that worked. Can we look at 7D705, please. This is a Drina Corps order of the 29th of May of 1995, signed by General Zivanovic, which indicates that he will command the forces from the forward command post. What can we see happening by this order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: This order is a tactical example of what I was referring to a minute ago. The Drina Corps command has issued an order stating that some of the Podrinje Detachment forces -- it was in fact a manoeuvres battalion, but these forces were to be used in a combat situation, and they were to be under the personal command of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we now look at 7D766.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The document in B/C/S looks like a telegram. Is that what it is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document followed on the other document, the order we saw a minute ago. This is a telegram that the commander of the Podrinje Detachment, Milan Jolovic, sent to the corps -- commander, rather, to the Pribicevac tactical group. He requested for certain reasons that one of his soldiers should be returned to Zvornik. He didn't ask for the soldier to be returned through the command of the Zvornik Brigade. He asked this to be done through the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we can leave that alone, then. Now, we're moving on to a very large topic, but we've got ten minutes left, so we'll begin it today. There's been an enormous amount of discussion in this case about the JNA brigade rules. Can I take it you are very familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: There really are very many rules that regulated the way that the JNA was to function. I'm familiar with most of them, but I wouldn't want to claim that I'm familiar with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it was probably either my fault or a translation difficulty. I'm really only concerned at this stage with the brigade rules of 1984. Are you familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the brigade rules. That represents one set of rules that regulate the way in which various brigades are to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to break into the topic today, I wonder if we could have in e-court P408 at page 1 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English. And the portion of -- thank you very much, thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who made these rules, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: These rules are part of the professional military literature that's available, and professionals made these rules. These brigade rules, well, they concern infantry brigades, motorised mountain brigades, marines, light brigades. These rules were created by the Infantry Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who or what is that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff of the JNA was organised in such a way that it insisted on several administrations. Occasionally, it would change the way it was organised, but as far as I can remember each arm of the army had its own administration that was responsible for it, in terms of technique and doctrine, and thus the Infantry Administration was responsible for matters relating to the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder now if we can go down to, as it were, the legal force, if any, of these rules. We can see that they are made pursuant to item 34(c) of the instructions on the preparation and use of professional military literature. What are the instructions on the preparation and use of professional military literature?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't now like to comment on the contents of these instructions, because it's not fresh in my mind, but these instructions, that state how and who should issue professional military textbooks that would be used in military academies, in military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is an instruction, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the word "instruction" speaks for itself. It says that one instructs someone to do something, or it tells someone how to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at P694, please, at page 12 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English. And this is a different version of the same document. It's just that in this version, the pages we have been looking at are mistranslated, so we prefer the accurate translation of those first two pages.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: You saw on the title page that these brigade rules concern five or six types of brigades, but there's one set of rules, and that's why in this introductory part it says that given the differences in terms of organisation and establishment and given the purposes of various groups within the infantry, the provisions of these rules must be applied in a creative way, and so on and so forth. I have to point out that the brigades of the VRS were even more different, in terms of organisation and establishment and in terms of their purpose, even more different than these five or six brigades that these rules refer to, and that is why it was essential to have a creative approach to the application of these rules. With your permission, in legal terms I'm a layman, but I know there is such a thing as criminal law, and I know that there are textbooks on criminal law. But punishment is meted out on the basis of the law, not on the basis of these textbooks. And so this textbook functions in a similar manner, like a textbook on criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll leave that there. There are just two or three things I'd like to deal with before we finish. At page 41, line 4 of the transcript, it's recorded that you describe Dragan Petkovic as the former commander of the Zvornik Brigade. We can give you the text of the answer, if you like. Did you describe him as the former commander or the formal commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: Up until a written order was drafted on my appointment and up until the report on the transfer of duties, Petkovic was officially the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. That was his status there, but he didn't have any actual control over the brigade. I was the person who had such control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 32, line 24, it's recorded that you said in Visegrad you went to the hydroelectric plant with your forces. The Muslim forces left the plant and withdrew to Gorazde. Is that what you said, "the Muslim forces," or something else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim forces were holding the hydroelectric power-plant, and they had opened up a gap, and a lot of water got through the gap and flooded a Muslim village. The person who opened up that gap, well, his house was destroyed by the water. The people in Bosnia are familiar with this affair. The name of the man involved is Murad Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well, thank you very much, General Pandurevic. We'll resume again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Thank you, General Pandurevic. As has just been stated, we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
